newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Fighting rages north of Kabul, no breakthrough seen.
newsitem.headline: Fighting rages north of Kabul, no breakthrough seen.

text.p: Heavy exchanges of rockets and artillery raged along the front line north of Kabul on Sunday but there was no sign of any breakthrough by either side in Afghanistan's bloody civil war.

Taleban militia gunners launched a barrage from Soviet-made artillery and multiple rocket launchers. They were aiming at the forces of the opposition alliance on the front lines 20 to 25 km (15 to 19 miles) north of Kabul.
The alliance responded with air attacks on Taleban positions.
An alliance plane also launched an air-raid on Kabul airport. A Taleban commander at the airport said there were no casulaties or damage.
The airport, used for both military and civilian flights, has been frequently targeted by alliance planes. However, there has been little reported damage and no casualties.
On the front line north of Kabul, opposition forces have been trying to capture a line of hills since their southward advance was halted by the Taleban in mid-October.
Despite numerous alliance attacks over recent weeks, there has been little significant change in the front.
The anti-Taleban alliance, made up of forces of the ousted government and fighters loyal to northern leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, has vowed to force the Taleban out of Kabul.

Representatives of the fundamentalist Taleban and General Dostum have met in the Pakistani capital Islamabad under the auspices of the United Nations to talk about the possibility of a peaceful settlement.
In the past, the Taleban radicals have been unwilling to compromise in peace talks, insisting that all other groups in Afghanistan surrender to them.

An Iranian radio station, monitored in Kabul on Saturday night, reported that a senior member of the Taleban, governor of the northwestern city of Herat Mullah Yar Mohammed had said the Afghan conflict could only be solved by war.
The accuracy of the report could not be verified.
Western observers in Kabul believe that the Taleban's recent string of victories, and particularly the capture of Kabul, will make them less ready to compromise in the search for peace.
The observers say that factional involvement in past UN-sponsored peace talks was largely a matter of form rather than substance.
They say the deadlock north of Kabul holds little hope for a quick end to Afghanistan's four-year-old civil conflict.
